entries.title: threads
entries.summary: Several flows of execution inside one process (pthreads).
entries.description: A **thread** is a unit of CPU use inside a process. All the threads of a process share the code, the global data, the heap and the open files; each has its own program counter, registers and **stack**, and an identifier (`pthread_t`). Compared with processes they are cheaper to create and to switch between, they share data with no copying, and they use several CPUs: but they also share every bug (one bad write corrupts the others) and they need **synchronisation** when they touch the same data. **User threads** are provided by a library (POSIX `pthread`); **kernel threads** by the operating system. Compile with `-pthread` (the course also writes `-lpthread`).
mistakes: Thinking that threads get their own copy of the globals (that is processes).

entries.title: pthread_create
entries.syntax:
int pthread_create(pthread_t *tid, const pthread_attr_t *attr,
                   void *(*start)(void *), void *arg);
entries.description: Creates a thread that runs `start(arg)`. The identifier is stored in `*tid`. `attr` selects attributes (`NULL` = defaults). `start` must be a function that takes and returns a `void *`; `arg` is how you give it data (the address of an `int`, of a struct...). Returns `0` on success, an error number otherwise (it does not set `errno`). The new thread may begin running before `pthread_create` returns.
mistakes: Passing `&i` of a loop counter: all threads see the same variable, which keeps changing. Give each thread its own argument (an array element).
Passing the address of a local variable that has gone out of scope when the thread reads it.

entries.title: pthread_join
entries.summary: Wait for a thread to end and get its result.
entries.description: Blocks until the thread `tid` ends. If `retval` is not `NULL`, it receives the value that the thread returned or passed to `pthread_exit` (a `void *`). Returns `0` or an error number. Every thread that is not *detached* should be joined once. (The course's slide writes the second parameter as `int **`; the right type is `void **`.) Whatever the thread wrote is visible to the joiner afterwards.
mistakes: Returning a pointer to a local variable of the thread: it is gone after the thread ends (use `malloc` or a struct of the caller).
Joining inside the loop that creates the threads: they then run one after another.

entries.title: pthread_exit
entries.summary: End the calling thread, optionally returning a value.
entries.description: Ends the calling thread; `value` is what `pthread_join` will receive. A `return value;` from the thread's function does exactly the same, so (course wording aside) threads do **not** have to end with `pthread_exit`. Calling `exit` instead ends the whole process, with all its threads; so does `return` from `main`.
mistakes: Calling `exit` from a thread when you only meant to end that thread.

entries.title: pthread_self
entries.summary: The identifier of the calling thread.
entries.description: Returns the `pthread_t` of the thread that calls it. Compare two identifiers with `pthread_equal`, not with `==` in portable code.
